catalog_quote: Word stress in Liŋŋit̯iɣ is predictable: the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed. Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster -- kápan short, ŋgóðRo black -- but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel -- ayóŋ I, alán sky, aðá crow.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable that has an onset consonant: word-initial syllable in consonant- or cluster-initial words, second syllable in vowel-initial words (the onsetless initial vowel is never stressed). Historically this is the Northern Paman shift of stress from the Proto-Paman initial syllable to the second syllable, with loss of *C1 (fascicle pp.167-168).
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; rule stated as exceptionless ('predictable'). Hale flags the segment inventory (not the stress rule) as 'extremely tentative'; data from ~2 weeks' fieldwork with one speaker (Sam Kerindun), 1960.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('word stress'); examples are isolated citation forms including an inflected pronoun (ayóŋ 'I'). Intonation/terminal pause contours treated separately in the next paragraph.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale's sketch describes Liŋŋit̯iɣ (Linngithigh proper) as recorded from one speaker, Sam Kerindun, at Aurukun in 1960; Hale states Linngithigh and Alngith (Alŋit̯, glottocode alng1239) 'are dialects of a single language, sharing 87 percent of basic vocabulary', but the stress statement and examples are Linngithigh only. Matches leni1238 directly.

new_statements.quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of initial syllables (*C1V1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it, is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*C2V2) in Paman stems.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement from Hale 1966 (AL 8(2):179: 'the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed'): the 1964 passage supplies the diachronic origin of that pattern (stress moved to the second proto-syllable, then the initial syllable was reduced or lost) and explicitly labels stress 'a strictly phonetic feature', which supports the 1966 claim that stress is predictable/non-contrastive. It does not mention syllable weight; the catalog record's classification weight is not supported by this work (see conflicts). The statement is about Northern Paman as a group, not about Linngithig alone; the paper is a classification/comparative report and has no phonology or…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A diachronic statement covering all Northern Paman languages (Linngithig is listed as group D, p. 252): primary stress, which Hale calls 'a strictly phonetic feature' (i.e. non-contrastive), shifted from the initial to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem (*C2V2), and this shift drove the loss of *C1 and the loss/reduction/metathesis of *V1. In the modern words the stressed syllable is therefore the reflex of the proto second syllable, which is the first consonant-initial syllable of the word: word-initial in words whose *V1 was lost (e.g. *kumpu > mpu 'urine', p. 258), second-syllable in words that kept a vowel reflex of *V1 (e.g. *wa:tYa > aδa 'crow', p. 258). No synchronic stress rule for Linngithig specifically is stated, and no stress marks appear in the Linngithig example forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. On the segmental side Hale notes that Uradhi and its sister dialects sometimes retain *C1 (p. 256), but Linngithig is stated to have lost *C1 invariably; the stress-shift statement itself is given for 'Paman stems' without exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964 spells the language Liŋŋit̯iɣ (scanned: 'Lingitiy') and locates it southwest of the Embley River and west of the Hey River in the Winduwinda area, from informants at Weipa/Aurukun in 1960 (p. 253); he groups it with Alngith (Alŋit̯) as Northern Paman group D (p. 252) and discusses the naming confusion with McConnel's Leningiti and Sharp's Lenngeti. The stress statement is made for Northern Paman / 'Paman stems' collectively, not for this variety in particular.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources on placement: Hale 1964 (stress shifted to the second syllable of the Proto-Paman stem, then the initial syllable was lost or reduced) and Hale 1966 (stress on the first vowel preceded by a consonant) describe the same outcome from diachronic and synchronic angles, and Blevins 2001 and Goedemans 1998 (already held by the project) repeat them second-hand. The one tension is inside the catalog itself: the catalog record for Linngithig carries classification weight, while the only primary statements (Hale 1964, 1966) give a positional rule with no reference to vowel length or coda; the 'weight' label is defensible only if it is meant as onset-sensitivity (Goedemans 1998 lists Linngithigh under 'stress is on the first postconsonantal syllable' and argues that this is not weight). Hale 1964 says nothing about weight, so it neither confirms nor directly refutes that label, but it gives no support for a quantity-sensitive reading.

tone.quote: Word stress in Liŋŋit̯iɣ is predictable: the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed. Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster -- kápan short, ŋgóðRo black -- but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel -- ayóŋ I, alán sky, aðá crow. Terminal pauses are #, characterized by a preceding fall in pitch, and #//, characterized by a preceding fall and rise. As is commonly the case in Australia, the first clause in di-clausal sentences normally, but not invariably, has the intonation associated with #// …
tone.summary: No lexical tone is described: word stress is predictable (first vowel after a consonant) and pitch figures only as a fall or fall-rise before terminal pauses, i.e. as intonation.
tone.says: No lexical tone is described: word stress is predictable (first vowel after a consonant) and pitch figures only as a fall or fall-rise before terminal pauses, i.e. as intonation.
